item.title: The 'Super Scam Me' Documentary Reveals Why Dating Scams Work
item.description:
Mating

The 'Super Scam Me' Documentary Reveals Why Dating Scams Work

Practically anyone can fall for dating scams. A new documentary shows us why.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • Rather than blaming victims of romance scams, we should understand how good scammers are at what they do.
  • Romance scammers are highly prevalent online, meaning that one is likely to quickly encounter them.
  • Scammers use love bombing to get target hooked and then exploit emotions like love and hope.
  • Awareness and quadruple checking everything is important. But so is not going at it alone.
In the new documentary "Super Scam Me," Emmy Award-winning Investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller assumed the alter ego of Mary Zelle online to attract and engage with romance scammers.
Source: Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images

Think you'd never fall for a romance scam—such as someone online telling you that he is Jon Bon Jovi and asking you to send him some crypto? Do you believe that anyone susceptible to such deception is simply stupid and gullible? Well, the documentary Super Scam Me, which premiers October 17 on National Geographic may change your mind and help you realize how easy it is to fall for a scammer who gives love a bad name.

In the documentary, Emmy-winning investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller reveals how such victims—including the woman who was fooled by a non-Bon Jovi—can actually be very intelligent and well-educated; It's just that scammers can be quite manipulative and opportunistic. van Zeller even goes undercover and assumes an alter ego named “Mary Zelle”—a middle-age antiques dealer—to allow herself to be lured in by scammers.

It Is Too Easy to Blame the Victim of Romance Scams

Van Zeller recently told me how she came up with the idea for the documentary about a year-and-a-half ago, after she had already reported extensively on scams. She found that others hearing her reporting would quickly "focus on the victims and how is it possible that they did this? Why would you give money to a stranger? How stupid could you be? And that really sort of frustrated me. So I wanted to turn the table and try to understand and focus on the actions of those scammers."

She thought that maybe the best way to look at this might be to "place myself at the center of all these scams and try to see it from the perspective of the victim as a person who sort of is immersed in the tactics and the strategies used by these scammers and show how professional, how good they are at what they do."

Romantic Scammers Are All Over the Place

So how long did it take for van Zeller—or rather "Mary Zelle"—to attract scammers? "Within literally minutes of me posting Mary Zelle online on dating websites and social media profiles, immediately I started being contacted by scammers," van Zeller explained. "It turns out that Mary Zelle was very, very popular on the dating websites."

What made Mary Zelle so popular? Well, she was a woman and seemed to be real—two things that will automatically attract a bunch of men online. But Zelle's profile also drew from a typical profile of a middle-aged woman—the most likely target for scammers—"even though I truly believe any one of us can be a victim of a scam," van Zeller says. "Men are also as likely to be victims of scans as women, but they're less likely to report it. But with me being a woman, we looked at middle-aged women who are recently divorced or with husbands passed away, and who sort of lead a lonely night life and are out there looking for love." How did van Zeller make it clear that Mary Zelle was living a lonely life? "I literally said that I was out there looking for love."

Love Bombing Can Be Effective, Especially During the Loneliness Epidemic

Once the profile was up, van Zeller admitted that the experience was essentially da bomb at first: "It was kind of fun to have your profile on dating websites and be love-bombed by all these people, especially since I've been married for 20 years." (Love bombing is when someone floods you with excessive affection, flattery, and attention to quickly establish your connection to, and dependency on, that person.)

As van Zeller pointed out, such love bombing can be particularly effective if you feel lonely—after all, we are in the midst of a loneliness epidemic that's been growing ever since the 1980s.

Romance Scammers Use a Variety of Manipulative Tactics

Love bombing is just the start of the manipulation. "When I actually started having a relationship, particularly with 'Mark' [someone who called himself Mark Turner], it became very draining very soon, emotionally draining as well, because I was playing a part," van Zeller explains. She described Mark as "very needy" — "he was constantly wanting to know how I was doing and showing me he would remember little details about conversations we had weeks before. He was making sure that I was arriving home safely and that I was eating my dinner and I was sort of taken care of and seen and cared for. This is the emotional manipulation that they're so good at"

This experience helped change van Zeller's viewpoint on romance scammers, from thinking that "they are exploiting people's ignorance or intelligence" to realizing that "they are exploiting the emotions that we all share—hope, fear, love, sometimes greed—and are very, very good at doing that. They're very good at understanding what is it that you need and what you're packing in your life." She added that "they have an incredible resource, a very rare resource on their hands, which is time. They devote a lot of time to you and a scam." As a result, "you don't think this person is a stranger," which makes it a lot easier for them to get something from you.

What Can Be Done About Romance Scammers

With so many scammers out there, van Zeller believes, "people should be more aware of what's happening. We should be giving people tips on how to protect themselves." She urges everyone to "double, triple, quadruple check everything," adding, "If it looks too good to be true, it is probably too good to be true."

However, she feels that the burden shouldn't all fall on you. "I think the onus lies on the government that is not doing enough to prevent these scams from happening. Social media companies and big tech companies are not doing enough either—or the banks, which have become essentially tools for these for these scammers." In others words, don't bank on your own abilities alone. Get help from friends and others. Otherwise, you could find yourself "living on a prayer" when it comes to love.

item.title: Can You Still Celebrate Friends You No Longer Speak To?
item.description:
Friends

Can You Still Celebrate Friends You No Longer Speak To?

In a world of ghosting and estrangement, we can still honor what once mattered.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows friendships change over time, often without conflict, as our social circles evolve.
  • A friendship doesn’t have to last forever for its memories to remain meaningful.
  • You can hold space for the past without reopening the door, allowing gratitude and boundaries to coexist.

Do you have photos from your past that you scroll past a little too quickly? A college roommate who stopped returning texts? A friend who landed on the other side of a political divide and made sure you knew it? Someone who simply vanished, with no explanation and no forwarding address for your emotions?

If so, you’re in good company. And I have a surprisingly low-tech suggestion to ease the ache these situations can sometimes cause—well, let’s say medium-tech.

Last Christmas, I received a digital picture frame. It took me until roughly spring to set it up. That was partly because the instructions seemed translated from a language not yet invented, and partly because of something I didn’t expect: hesitation.

As I loaded decades' worth of photos, I found myself stopping on certain faces. These were people I no longer speak to. Some I had to step away from. Some stepped away from me. Some left without a word. Several of them stood beside me at my wedding, which made for an interesting—and unexpectedly emotional—slideshow.

My first instinct was to quietly delete certain photos and curate the past to match the present. Then I paused long enough to ask myself: Does the fact that someone isn’t in my life now erase what they meant to me then?

Friendships Have Seasons

It helps to know this is normal. In a seven-year study of more than 600 Dutch adults, sociologist Gerald Mollenhorst and colleagues found that while the size of people’s social networks stayed remarkably stable, the membership didn’t. Only about 30 percent of the people participants turned to for personal conversations or practical help still held that role seven years later. And a key reason relationships ended wasn’t conflict. It was losing the shared settings that brought people together in the first place.

In other words, our social life doesn't have a permanent cast. It's more like a long-running series. Characters get written out. Some exits are dramatic. Others happen quietly, offscreen, between seasons.

Looking Back Can Pull Us Forward

So I loaded the pictures—and the sometimes triggering memories—into the frame along with all the others. And something unexpected happened: When one of those faces flashed by, I didn’t feel the jolt of resentment or hurt I’d braced for. I felt something warmer: the memory of laughing until it hurt, the road trip, the night someone showed up exactly when I needed them, the friend holding my hand behind my back while I stood near the altar listening to my wedding officiant.

This tracks with research on nostalgia. Across seven studies, psychologists Tim Wildschut, Constantine Sedikides, and colleagues found that nostalgic memories typically center on people we’ve been close to and meaningful moments. Experiencing nostalgia bolstered people’s sense of social connection, raised positive self-regard, and lifted mood. That doesn’t mean it’s pure sunshine. Nostalgia is often bittersweet, especially when a relationship ended without much explanation or even painfully. But on balance, nostalgia appears to be something we can draw strength from, rather than somewhere we get stuck.

The Grudge Tax

Of course, remembering someone fondly isn’t the same as forgiving them for what happened. You don’t have to excuse every hurt to appreciate a happy memory. But for the hurts we’re ready to set down, research hints at a benefit. In a study from Hope College, Charlotte van Oyen Witvliet and colleagues asked participants to think about someone who had genuinely wronged them. Participants either rehearsed the hurt and nursed a grudge or imagined empathy and forgiveness. In the moment, grudge-holding produced more negative emotion and measurable increases in heart rate, blood pressure, and facial muscle tension, and some of those effects lingered briefly after the exercise ended. Forgiving thoughts, on the other hand, brought lower stress responses and a greater sense of control.

Here’s the part I love: No one in that study picked up the phone. The forgiveness happened entirely in their own heads.

Boundaries and Gratitude Can Share a Frame

That’s exactly what this digital frame taught me. Celebrating what someone once meant to me isn’t the same as inviting them back. Some of those boundaries exist for good reasons, and they’re staying put. There will be no reunion brunch and no “thinking of you” text at 11 p.m. But I can hold the boundary and the gratitude at the same time. I loved these people once. That love was real. It still counts.

Now the digital frame cycles through decades of my life, and when a photo features someone who was once an important part of it, I notice less sting and more appreciation. Call it acceptance on a 10-minute rotation.

So if there’s a photo or, more importantly, a memory you’ve been skipping past, consider letting it stay. Sit with it. Breathe it in. See if you can find some appreciation, perhaps even peace. You don’t have to reopen the door to honor what happened in the room.

item.title: The Paradox of Sex in Romantic Relationships
item.description:
Sex

The Paradox of Sex in Romantic Relationships

If sex is ‘just sex,’ why does sexual infidelity feel like a profound betrayal?

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • Sex may appear superficial, yet sexual infidelity is often experienced as love's deepest violation.
  • Change tends to fuel sexual desire, while familiarity often strengthens romantic attachment.
  • Sexual afterglow may contribute more to lasting relationship satisfaction than orgasm alone.
  • Love and sex exist on an intimacy continuum rather than as simple opposites.

Sex is often treated as one of the least profound aspects of enduring romantic love, yet sexual infidelity is experienced as one of love's deepest violations. How can we explain this paradox?

The Paradox of Sex

The paradox of sex in romantic relationships is that its positive contribution to a flourishing, enduring relationship may sometimes seem limited, providing largely momentary physical pleasure. Yet when it violates an exclusive bond, sex can carry enormous destructive power. Why does something often dismissed as "just sex" become the ultimate romantic betrayal?

Romantic love rests on two major evaluations: (a) a partner's attractiveness and (b) the praiseworthiness of the partner's traits and achievements. The first is typically expressed through sexual desire; the second deepens friendship, caring, and admiration. Although these evaluations are distinct, they often reinforce each other. Attractive partners are frequently perceived as possessing more admirable qualities, while admired partners often become more attractive. This duality reflects the ambiguous nature of sex: It may provide immediate physical pleasure while also strengthening a profound emotional bond.

To understand this paradox, I examine five related issues: the ambiguous nature of sex, the roles of change and familiarity, the distinction between making love and having sex, the intimacy continuum, and sexual afterglow.

Source: Ron Lach/Pexels

The Ambiguous Nature of Sex

Sex can be viewed as serving two primary functions: bodily pleasure and relational connection. From the first perspective, sex need not threaten romantic love. Hence the familiar claim: "I had sex with someone else, but I still love you." Yet sex can also embody intimacy, exclusivity, desire, and belonging.

A sexual interaction may be physically brief yet psychologically significant. A kiss, sexual encounter, or affair may last only minutes or hours, yet its meaning can be enormous because it violates an important relational boundary. Many people regard sexual infidelity as the ultimate betrayal, while others defend it by saying, "It was only sex. It meant nothing." But this defense raises an obvious question: If it meant nothing, why was the relationship worth risking for it?

Change and Familiarity

"The more I see you, the more I want you. Somehow this feeling just grows and grows." —Chris Montez

"Weirdly, I want the unpleasant situation between me and my husband to change. But then again, I would not have an excuse for a hot lover. Just being honest." —A married woman

Emotions typically arise when we perceive significant changes in our own circumstances or in the lives of those close to us. From an evolutionary perspective, attending to change is adaptive because change may signal opportunity or threat. Once we adapt to a new situation, however, its emotional impact often diminishes (Ben-Ze’ev, 2019).

This tendency may appear to work against enduring romantic love. Yet familiarity has its own emotional value. In long-term relationships characterized by commitment and shared activities, familiarity can deepen intimacy and romantic meaning. Change tends to ignite sexual desire, whereas familiarity often nurtures romantic attachment.

Making Love and Having Sex

Although making love usually involves sex, not every sexual encounter can be described as making love. Compared to merely having sex, making love is often more patient, emotionally intimate, and relationally significant. A key difference concerns time. Making love reflects what might be called a patient heart, one that values both present enjoyment and future connection. Simply having sex is more likely to emphasize immediate gratification.

Making love also tends to foster greater intimacy. It involves shared attention, responsiveness, and emotional resonance between partners. In such encounters, giving may become as important as receiving, encouraging a more other-centered form of sexual interaction.

The Intimacy Continuum

"Last night I had sex with my husband, but he did not actually touch me. He just penetrated me. I was so sad I could cry." —A married woman

"I cannot engage in lip-kissing with men I have sex with unless there is profound intimacy. Kissing other body parts, including sexual organs, feels less intimate." —A married woman

The connection between love and sex comes in many forms. Commercial sex illustrates that the two can be separated, while the husband's behavior described above shows that emotional disconnection can occur even within marriage. Love and sex therefore exist on an intimacy continuum rather than as simple opposites.

‎Elizabeth Bernstein (2007) coined the term bounded authenticity to describe the sale and purchase of authentic emotional and physical connection in certain forms of sex work. This differs from purely impersonal sexual release. Bernstein notes that some sex workers attempt to create genuine feelings of desire, esteem, and emotional connection, giving clients a sense of being valued and wanted. Accordingly, commercial sex need not always involve what people dismiss as "counterfeit intimacy."

Sexual Afterglow

"While having an affair, I was sexually aroused and began noticing other men noticing me. Even my husband seemed more attracted to me. When it rains, it pours." —A married woman

"My married lover became emotionally distant the moment he ejaculated. The speed with which he withdrew emotionally and physically was astonishing." —A divorcee

Sexual afterglow refers to the positive feelings that linger after a satisfying sexual encounter. Research suggests that these lingering feelings, rather than orgasm alone, play an important role in shaping attitudes toward one's partner. Although less intense than orgasm, afterglow may contribute more to long-term relationship satisfaction. Spouses who experience stronger afterglow report greater marital satisfaction, suggesting that afterglow may help strengthen pair bonds. While orgasm is the clearest expression of sexual intensity, the affectionate interaction that follows sex may do more to deepen a romantic connection. Studies indicate that sexual afterglow lasted at least one day on average and is associated with greater marital satisfaction. The enduring effects of sex, rather than the immediate climax alone, may therefore be especially important for relationship quality and longevity (Breedin, O. W., et al. 2025; Danovich, 2017).

Concluding Thoughts

Love and sex are two central forces in romantic life. Their relationship is complex: sometimes they reinforce one another, and sometimes they pull us in different directions. There is no simple formula for balancing them. Yet relationships are most likely to flourish when sex and love complement rather than compete with each other.

The significance of sex depends less on the physical act itself than on the meaning it acquires within a relationship. Sex may be brief, physically, and seemingly superficial, yet at the same time psychologically and romantically profound. This is precisely why, despite being described as "just sex," it can become one of love's deepest expressions—or one of its deepest betrayals.

item.title: Lead Like a Follower, Follow Like a Leader
item.description:
Leadership

Lead Like a Follower, Follow Like a Leader

The art of collaboration, in musical performance or the workplace.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • Psychological research shows an "unconstrained vision" can unlock creative breakthroughs in workplace teams.
  • Open-minded collaboration requires leaders to explore valid opposing viewpoints rather than force agreement.
  • True teamwork requires flexible leadership that knows when to guide a project and when to follow others.
  • Studies on group dynamics reveal that accepting constructive friction leads to superior outcomes.
Source: Rod Judkins

Leonard Bernstein stepped out to address the audience at Carnegie Hall. The audience knew something must be wrong. He was set to conduct Brahms’s D Minor Concerto with the New York Philharmonic and soloist Glenn Gould. The audience was right: This performance became one of classical music’s most controversial and instructive moments of collaboration. It highlighted the positive impact of what psychologists call ‘the unconstrained vision’.

Sometimes, we think we know exactly how a project should develop, only to find our colleagues have different views. This kind of clash happens often at work. I’ve seen it myself when pitching book proposals to publishers. They accept my ideas, but have different views on how to develop them. Real collaboration means accepting that other people’s ideas can make the project better than anything we could do alone.

Bernstein was a major figure in music, famous for his creative approach. He wrote the music for West Side Story, which changed musical theatre with its serious story, complex music, and attention to social issues. Bernstein was also an innovative conductor who had invited the well-known pianist Gould to play the solo in Brahms’s concerto.

When people work together, they need to agree on what they are trying to achieve. In early rehearsals, Gould told Bernstein, "Oh boy, have I got some surprises for you; I have made such discoveries about this piece." Bernstein liked bold ideas, but Gould’s suggestions were almost too much for him. As the conductor, Bernstein had to balance trying new things, supporting his team, and meeting the expectations of an audience that had paid a lot to be there.

These kinds of conflicts are tough for both leaders and team members. Most of us have seen it at work: People get stuck on their own ideas and don’t listen to each other, which leads to a standstill. This can happen in any team project, whether it’s architects designing a building, co-founders starting a business, or marketers planning a campaign. For example, one architect might want a simple design, while another prefers something more decorative. This disagreement can cause problems, but if everyone stays open-minded, it can lead to a much better outcome.

On the night of the concert, things reached a breaking point. Bernstein walked onto the stage to loud applause, but Gould was not with him. Their creative differences had grown so big that Bernstein thought the audience needed to know what was going on.

Source: Rod Judkins

"You are about to hear an 'unorthodox performance'. A performance distinctly different from any I’ve ever heard, or even dreamt of, for that matter," Bernstein said. He went on to say that he disagreed with Gould’s conception, but posed a key question on collaborative leadership: "What am I doing conducting it? I’m conducting it because Mr Gould is so valid and serious an artist that I must take seriously anything he conceives in good faith, and his conception is interesting enough so that I feel you should hear it, too."

Bernstein built up the excitement, turning his colleague’s different opinion into a joint experience. "Why do I not make a minor scandal, get a substitute soloist, or let an assistant conduct?" he asked. "Because I am fascinated, glad to have the chance for a new look at this much-played work." Gould then came onstage, and together they gave a performance that people still talk about.

A theory that helps explain the benefits of open-minded teamwork, like Bernstein’s, comes from economist Thomas Sowell’s book A Conflict of Visions. He describes how two well-meaning colleagues can quickly become opponents because they have two basic ways of thinking: the constrained vision and the unconstrained vision.

  • The Constrained Vision: People with this mindset believe human nature doesn’t change. They prefer proven methods, follow tradition, and stick to routines instead of trying new ideas.
  • The Unconstrained Vision: People with this mindset see processes as flexible and improvable. They get frustrated by strict workplace rules that limit inventive problem-solving. They accept mistakes because they know errors are part of coming up with new ideas together.
Source: Rod Judkins

Bernstein’s actions show how to use an unconstrained vision when working with others. It’s hard enough to create music with an open mind, but it’s even harder to stay flexible in everyday work, where routines can make us feel stuck.

That’s why it stands out when colleagues in disciplines like software, business, or science move past rigid thinking to support each other’s ideas. For example, Intuit co-founder Scott Cook noticed that his team was so focused on technical details that they neglected the user experience. By encouraging his team to work together more creatively, they changed personal finance management with easy-to-use products like Quicken, QuickBooks, and TurboTax.
Bernstein was open to exploring ideas he didn’t agree with, which is a rare but important skill in teamwork. He shows us that real collaboration means knowing when to lead and when to follow.

item.title: Less Common Presentations and Overlooked Features of ADHD
item.description:
ADHD

Less Common Presentations and Overlooked Features of ADHD

Findings from the most up-to-date research about ADHD and its presentations.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • The ADHD symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity show up in often unrecognized ways.
  • Emotional dysregulation, rejection sensitivity, and the importance of interests are key ADHD experiences.
Individual playing with a fidget
Source: Andrej Lišakov / Unsplash

In honor of ADHD Awareness Month, this post focuses on the less common presentations of ADHD symptoms and commonly overlooked presentations of ADHD. First, I would like to address the uncommon presentations of ADHD. As many of you know, the symptoms for diagnosing ADHD include inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. These symptoms have often been conceptualized in stereotypically male terms, but in recent years, we have become more aware of their varied presentations.

Inattention

Inattention might not simply be being very daydreamy or spacey; it can also be a desire to talk about and focus on our interests, and difficulty paying attention when we're not doing things that interest us. In fact, the name Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder is a misnomer, since we actually don't have a deficit of attention. Still, in fact, we have difficulty regulating our attention when we are not interested.

Impulsivity

When we think of looking for impulsivity, we often think again of the stereotypical young white male who has trouble regulating their behavior in the classroom. However, impulsivity might show up in other ways, such as difficulty regulating speech, interrupting, or difficulty stopping a preferred behavior—such as scrolling social media, playing video games, or another activity that is compelling but may not be healthy or intentionally chosen for the setting.

Hyperactivity

We often think of hyperactivity as physical hyperactivity. However, this can show up in a variety of ways, such as doing chores restlessly, always doing something, or always needing to be on the go. Or it can look like verbal hyperactivity or even mental hyperactivity, where someone has many, many thoughts and may even seem to be "stuck in their head."

Masking and Broader Definitions

As you think about these symptoms and look for them, please keep in mind the broader definitions of these terms and how they show up in different individuals. It's also important to recognize that many people try to avoid appearing to have challenges in these areas, so they may go to great lengths to mask their behavior and fit in. This can cause symptoms to appear in further, unexpected ways (Mutti-Driscoll, 2026).

Overlooked Features of ADHD

Now I would like to talk about some overlooked features of ADHD that are gaining recognition through the efforts and discussion of Dr. William Dodson.

  • Interest-Driven Nervous Systems: The first overlooked feature of ADHD is that people with ADHD have interest-driven nervous systems. This relates to the criteria of attention, which, as discussed, needs a broader framing as a difficulty with attention regulation when someone is not interested. Interests are very important for people with ADHD, so a great accommodation for yourself or others is to center your interests as much as possible.
  • Emotional Hyperarousal: The second overlooked feature of ADHD is emotional hyperarousal. The challenges of emotion regulation in ADHD—which are sadly not part of the diagnostic criteria in the United States at present—are gaining further attention. Many books are addressing the higher highs and lower lows of people with ADHD. This is what can make someone with ADHD more excitable than the average person, and depressed moods can come on quickly for them, and also last longer, than for others.
  • Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria: Rejection sensitive dysphoria (Dodson et al., 2024) is also a common experience for people with ADHD; it is experienced by 90% of people with ADHD. This is the intense experience of criticism, teasing, or the perception that someone has failed. This experience can be so intense that it feels physically painful and entirely overwhelming for those who experience it. For 30% of individuals, this is the most challenging aspect of ADHD (Neff, 2023).

Diagnostic Considerations, Impact, and Masking

Research is revealing that ADHD shows up in ways that we may have never thought possible when we fell into stereotypes of who has ADHD and how ADHD manifests. I hope that this discussion will help you identify ADHD more effectively and broadly in the people that you care about.

Another thing to keep in mind is that ADHD is only diagnosed in individuals who present challenges. These challenges have likely been present since childhood and show up in two or more settings in a person's life. Of course, what it means to be significantly impaired is debatable and really hinges upon the person's own experience and those around them being able to provide insight into what impact ADHD has on the individual's life.

If someone is effective at masking, these effects may be difficult to discern, and the individual may need to weigh in heavily on whether these challenges are significant and how they are experiencing their life. In some cases, individuals have masked so much that they can't even tell they're impacted. In such cases, reflecting on articles like this one may help a person determine whether they want to seek support and diagnostic insight into their experiences.

Conclusion

Understanding ADHD requires us to look beyond traditional stereotypes and recognize the nuanced ways it impacts people's daily lives. By expanding our understanding of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity—and honoring features such as interest-driven nervous systems, emotional hyperarousal, and rejection-sensitive dysphoria—we can foster greater self-compassion and offer better support to those around us. Whether you recognize these traits in yourself or a loved one, taking time to learn about these broader presentations is a meaningful step toward advocacy, self-discovery, and finding strategies that truly align with how your brain works.

item.title: How to Live Well Past 100 Years
item.description:
Aging

How to Live Well Past 100 Years

Research identifies the factors that impact the joy of aging well.

Posted October 17, 2026

Key points
  • The will to live is a positive factor that transcends gender, age, and comorbidities.
  • Continuing to enjoy life in later years depends on health, viewpoints, and absence of pain.
  • Socially, having a confidant is particularly important to centenarians.
Source: Image by David Sánchez-Medina Calderón from Pixabay

Many of us are familiar with the reminder, “Life is short.” Not so, for some people. According to the members of the Centenarians’ Club, the experience of living past 100 depends on quality of life.

The Century Club

Lia Araújo et al. (2021) studied a sample of 121 centenarians, examining attitudes and life satisfaction at an advanced age.[i] They began by acknowledging that one predictor for survival into ripe old age is a will to live—a factor that transcends gender, age, or comorbidities. Yet they also note that at an advanced age, life satisfaction and positive attitudes are tempered by longing for death. They sought to add to existing data by exploring the factors associated with centenarians' will to live.

Of their sample, 31.4% expressed a willingness to live longer, 30.6% did not, and 38% had no clear position on the matter. Yet they found that participants’ answers depended on the presence of other factors. The most common factors cited as reasons for reluctance to live longer were uselessness, loss of meaning annoyance, loneliness, and disconnection. Factors associated with being willing to live longer were good health, positive valuation of life, having a confidant, and reduced frequency of pain. Reference to God, however, was also mentioned by centenarians in all three groups.

Divine Providence and Desire to Live

Significantly, almost all study participants justified their lack of answer about continuing to live by mentioning God, stating that their time remaining was not in “their hands,” but out of their control. Araújo et al. note this is consistent with the belief that a sense of control “through the sacred” may arrive when life appears to be out of control. They note that older individuals who accept declining control over their environment and focus instead on an ability to control their own internal states and behaviors have better adjustment as they age. This group had a satisfaction with life score approximating the group who were willing to live longer.

Regarding the reference to God also being present in the other two groups, Araújo et al. note that religion and spirituality are important within the lives of older adults, as a method of finding meaning later in life. It is therefore associated with how long someone desires to live. They recognize that studying centenarians has confirmed the positive impact religion and spirituality have on well-being, a factor that has heightened significance within members of this age group who may lack to basic resources. Prior research has also found that religiosity was a major theme driving adapting and coping for centenarians.

Factors Impacting Living Well After 100

Regarding the specific factors that impact enjoyment of life in later years, Araújo et al. found many that we might expect: health, including the frequency of pain; social life, including having friends and confidants; and well-being—having a positive valuation of life. Accordingly, they note that the will to live depends on both external and interpersonal dynamics, in terms of having social networks, good health. as well as healthy self-perceptions.

Araújo et al. also found it significant that certain conditions did not significantly impact the will to live. These included health conditions, fatigue, and capacity to function. This is good news, suggesting that older adults facing physical challenges may nonetheless be about to maintain a state of subjective well-being.

Araújo et al. recognize that in advanced age, some purposes in life become more difficult to fulfill, such as creating and pursuing future goals or feeling useful—variables that are important, specifically as they relate to the unwillingness to live. On the other hand, they note that the will to live creates strong, direct effects on factors relating to subjective well-being such as satisfaction with aging and life.

The Enduring Satisfaction of Social Life

Social factors contribute to meaning in life among an elderly population, with relationships and sources of support of particular utility to centenarians. Araújo et al. note that at this advanced age, many people have lost friends and relatives, which reduces one’s social and familial circle. Yet in their study, the only social variable they found to be significantly linked with will to live was the number of friends participants had as confidants. They conclude that apparently, for this age group, the value of social networks is one of support rather than size. They note that having a confidant is a way for centenarians to compensate for loss and enhance well-being. Araújo et al. also note that, conversely, social disconnection and loneliness decreased the will to live, and made people feel more like a burden.

Apparently, living well past 100 depends on living with faith, family, and friends, appreciating the richness of the past, and celebrating every positive aspect of the present.

item.title: Catch-42: Waiting for Meaning
item.description:
Philosophy

Catch-42: Waiting for Meaning

Finding meaning in life remains a major goal for many. Psychology can help with the pursuit.

Posted October 17, 2026

Riddle: I slip when you chase me

I grin when you ask

Demand one neat answer

I vanish in laughs

Everything around us seems to change faster than we can make sense of it. How does that affect our search for meaning? The UCLA American Freshman survey1 has been asking incoming US college students about their life goals every year since 1966. Developing a meaningful philosophy of life showed the largest decline across generations, from its position as a top value in the late 60s for more than 80% of entering freshmen to just around 45% of millennials endorsing it as a priority. In 2019, the same Freshman Survey2 revealed that half of students still endorsed developing a meaningful philosophy of life as essential, but it was strongly overshadowed by 84% of respondents reporting "being very well off financially" as the most important goal (which might be a meaning in itself ).

Trying to understand such profound changes in the quest for meaning, I went looking for someone in charge of the meaning of life, only to learn that the position has been vacant for about 2,500 years. Fortunately, there was someone closer to home to poke about it: my colleague Éva Kállay, a psychologist at Babeș-Bolyai University who studies meaning in life and psychological well-being. Hoping for a neat answer (ideally, a number), I brought her some of my questions.

The ultimate question might yield no answer.
Source: Pexels / panumas nikhomkhai

Laura Visu-Petra: Why is the meaning of life such an impossible quest?

Éva Kállay: In The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, hyperintelligent pan-dimensional beings commission Deep Thought, a supercomputer, to determine the answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything4.

After 7.5 million years of computation, the long-awaited answer to the ultimate question finally arrives: The meaning of everything is … 42.

The response is met with astonishment and disbelief. How could the most powerful supercomputer ever built produce an answer that seems so utterly meaningless?

But Deep Thought is perplexed, too—by its creators’ reactions. The problem, it explains, is not the answer. The problem is that nobody knows the correct question: Only when you know the question will the answer make sense.

So, perhaps our real difficulty is not that we lack answers. Perhaps we have never asked the right question. And yet, this has not stopped us from looking outside ourselves for conclusive answers.

Like Beckett’s characters, Vladimir and Estragon, who wait through two acts for a Godot who never comes, we keep waiting for something that promises to make everything clear, but never quite arrives4.

Behind this seemingly futile exercise lie questions as old as humanity:

Why are we here?

Do we matter?

Why do we suffer?

What is the meaning of our lives?

For thousands of years philosophers, theologians, and more recently psychologists have wrestled to answer these questions. Yet, they remain as compelling, and elusive, as ever5. And for good reason. In what appears to be an infinite universe, whether our existence has an ultimate (or cosmic) meaning remains one of the greatest mysteries.

LVP: So, what can psychologists tell us?

EK: Fortunately, by reframing the question, psychology throws us a lifeline. Instead of asking about the grand meaning of life (traditionally the realm of philosophy and theology), it investigates how people experience, construct and ascribe meaning to their own lives. While the meaning of life remains an abstraction, meaning in life is a personal psychological experience, one that can be observed, discussed, and measured.

When we look at the details, our everyday lives become full of meaning6—we speak of meaningful memories, relationships, experiences, work, achievements.

LVP: What is a meaningful life made of?

EK: Most contemporary psychological perspectives identify three core components5,7.

Coherence is the sense that life is understandable—that events, relationships, and ideas fit together into something comprehensible, rather than a series of random events happening to us8.

Purpose is the compass and engine. It gives us both the direction and the energy to pursue what we believe matters9.

Significance is the belief that our existence matters, and that our absence would make a difference10.

So, a meaningful life is different from a collection of meaningful moments. It is the experience that those moments belong to a life story that makes sense, that is going somewhere, and is worth something.

LVP: Does it really matter whether life feels meaningful?

EK: The answer is surprisingly straightforward. Decades of research consistently show that people who experience their lives as meaningful report better physical, psychological, and social well-being11. A recent meta-analysis combining data from nearly half a million people, some followed for more than 30 years, found that a stronger sense of purpose predicted a substantially lower risk of dying over the study period12.

But the absence of meaning in life is equally revealing.

LVP: Why? What happens when life stops making sense?

EK: Most of us carry an implicit and rarely examined narrative of how the world works: We are taught to believe that good deeds are rewarded and bad ones punished, that people are broadly trustworthy, and that bad things do not happen to good people. Traumatic experiences can break the coherence of that account. When reality no longer fits the story we have lived by, we are forced to rewrite it. If we cannot, a sense of meaninglessness may set in, accompanied by anxiety, depression, or hopelessness13.

After the tragic loss of his teenage son, musical artist Nick Cave created heart-wrenching songs about how meaning is lost and replaced by a whirlpool of repetitiveness to cope with the pain:

I knew the world it would stop spinning now since you’ve been gone
I used to think that when you died you kind of wandered the world
In a slumber till you crumbled, were absorbed into the earth
Well I don’t think that anymore, the phone it rings no more
The song the song it spins it spins now since 1984
The song the song the song it spins its been spinning now

Research has mainly asked whether meaning in life is present or absent. But there is also a third dimension, in which people actively search for (a new) meaning14. The search for meaning is not characterized by serene reflection, but by an intense effort to find meaning that would make everything comprehensible again. Searching for renewed meaning is not comfortable. It comes with anxiety and rumination15, a restlessness that is not incidental but part of the process through which we rebuild our understanding of the world16.

LVP: And where does this meaning come from?

EK: One line of research has mapped the domains we draw on. Schnell17 identified 26 sources of meaning, grouped in higher-order dimensions: self-transcendence (e.g., religiosity, spirituality), self-actualization (e.g., development, freedom), order (e.g., tradition, morality), well-being, and relatedness (e.g., relationships, love, community).

A second line of research asks what strengthens the experience of meaning in life5. Positive affect, social belonging, religious faith, and routine were all found to play an important role in these processes. Meaning seems to be supplied less by grand certainties than by small regularities: how we shape our everyday lives and how we mark our holidays.

LVP: How do we find our sources of meaning?

EK: Modern life is full of competing, often conflicting, and sometimes supposedly scientific prescriptions about how we should live18.

So, just like the American Freshmen study revealed, we look for meaning in (financial) success, status, relationships, recognition, personal growth, and countless other pursuits. Yet this abundance of possible sources can itself become paralyzing19, leaving us uncertain which of them truly matters to us or defines our quest. It also raises a difficult question: Are we on a path that is genuinely our own?

The risk is that, under the pressure of cultural expectations and constant comparisons, we may adopt meanings that are socially valued but personally hollow. The “Choose life” monologue from the movie Trainspotting (1996) shows Renton reciting a long list of the conventional goals society offers (career, family, appliances, mortgage) and mocking them as a package deal people sign up for without thinking.

LVP: So, if we put the borrowed goals aside, the quest for meaning might become itself confusing. Was Deep Thought onto something?

EK: Deep Thought was right about one thing: If you do not know the question, there is little point in contemplating the answer. Psychology’s contribution may lie not in providing answers to our big existential question, but in helping us ask better, if smaller questions that ultimately might have to be asked in the first person:

What holds my life together?

To whom does my life matter?

Where is my life going?

Takeaway

Eva's answers make me understand that the active quest for meaning is not pointless. After all, engaging freely and creatively with all questions sent by his fellow human beings has helped artists like Nick Cave go through grief, and share that "there is a way out" in moving towards new meanings. He describes it vividly in his response from the Red Hand Files to the direct question sent by one of his readers: "What is the point in life?":20

We are capable of the greatest atrocities and the deepest sufferings, all culminating in a vast, collective grief. This is our shared condition. […] This is where meaning establishes itself, within the connectedness, nested in our shared suffering.

I believe we are meaning-seeking creatures, and these feelings of meaning, relational and connective, are almost always located within kindness. Kindness is the force that draws us together […] despite our collective state of loss, and our potential for evil, there exists a great network of goodness, knitted together by countless everyday human kindnesses.

Through kindness we slant, shockingly and miraculously, toward meaning. We discover, in that smallest gesture of goodwill laid at the feet of our mutual and monumental loss, the point.”
